Estimate population quantiles from a sample

Source: R/quantile.R
ht_quantile.Rd

ht_quantile() estimates quantiles of y, such as the median or the quartiles, from the Hajek estimate of its distribution function, F(t) = sum(w * (y <= t)) / sum(w) with w = 1 / pi, and gives each a Woodruff confidence interval and a standard error from the design's own variance estimator.

Usage

ht_quantile(
  sample,
  y,
  probs = 0.5,
  by = NULL,
  variance = c("auto", "analytic", "jackknife", "none"),
  level = 0.95,
  df = NULL
)

Arguments

sample

A data frame returned by draw() with weights = TRUE. See "Which columns are read".

y

The variable: a numeric column name of sample, or a numeric vector as long as sample. A logical y is refused, since its quantiles are 0 or 1; ht_mean() estimates the share that is TRUE.

probs

The probabilities, each from 0 to 1, such as 0.5 for the median or c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75) for the quartiles.

by

Optional column name(s) in sample defining domains. When given, the result is one row per domain. See "Domains". A column named like one of the table's own, such as n or se, is refused.

variance

How to compute it. "auto" uses the design's own estimator (see "Variance") and falls back to the jackknife when that declines; "analytic" insists on the design's own estimator, returning NA with the reason in note rather than falling back; "jackknife" uses the jackknife, and returns NA with the reason in note for systematic and Poisson samples, where it does not apply; "none" skips it. The result reports which was used in method, and "none" when nothing could produce a figure.

level

Confidence level for the interval.

df

Degrees of freedom for the interval. NULL uses the design's (see "Confidence intervals"); Inf gives a normal interval; otherwise a single number of 1 or more.

Value

For one probability without by, a list of class drawn_quantile with a print() method, holding quantile, the estimate; prob; variable, the name of y when it is a column name, else NULL; cdf and cdf_se, the estimated distribution function at the estimate and its standard error; steps, the estimated distribution function as the sorted sampled values x and the share of the weight F at or below each, which confint() reads to form the interval at another level; and variance, se, ci, level, alternative (always "two.sided"), df, n, n_random, design, deff, method, note and unreachable as for ht_total(), with ci_scale "woodruff".

For several probabilities, or with by, a drawn_by table with a row for each domain and probability: the by columns, prob, n, quantile, variance, se, ci_lower, ci_upper and method.

Both have coef(), vcov(), confint(), as.data.frame() and tidy() methods, as described under "Working with the result" in ht_total(). confint() at another level carries the interval for F(q) at that level back through the quantile rule. vcov() holds the variances, and NA for the covariances between quantiles, which are not estimated.

The quantile rule

The estimate at p is the smallest sampled value of y whose estimated distribution function is p or more, which inverts the step function F without interpolating between sampled values. It is always a value some sampled row has. This is the rule of survey::svyquantile(qrule = "math"), survey's default, and with equal weights it is stats::quantile(type = 1), apart from the tolerance below. p = 0 gives the smallest sampled value and p = 1 the largest.

A share of the weight equal to p can come out of the sums a rounding error below p, so a share within 1e-9 below p counts as reaching it. A p that is a rounding error above a share therefore gives the value at that share. seq(0, 1, 0.01)[71], which is 0.7 plus a rounding error, gives the 21st of 30 equally weighted values, where stats::quantile(type = 1) and survey::svyquantile() give the 22nd.

Interval and standard error

The interval is Woodruff's (1952). At the estimate q, F(q) is a Hajek mean of the indicator y <= q, and its variance is the variance of the total of the linearised residuals ((y <= q) - F(q)) / N_hat, with N_hat = sum(w), from the design's own estimator, as for ht_mean(). "Variance" and "Confidence intervals" in ht_total() describe the estimators, the fallback to the jackknife, the degrees of freedom and the notes. The interval F(q) plus or minus t standard errors, with t on the design's degrees of freedom, is carried back through the quantile rule, so its ends are the estimated quantiles at its two ends. The standard error is the interval's width divided by 2 t, and variance is its square. cdf and cdf_se in the result hold F(q) and its standard error.

Where the interval for F(q) runs below 0 or above 1, the sample bounds the quantile on one side only. That end of ci is then NA, and so are se and variance, with a note.

At the largest sampled value F(q) is 1 and its residuals are 0, so its estimated variance is 0 whatever the spread of y, and the interval would have no width. A quantile there, which a p close to 1 or a y with one value gives, gets no standard error, with a note, unless every frame row the design can reach was taken with certainty, when it is exact. A quantile whose sampled rows lie in one primary sampling unit gets none either, as a Hajek mean does, because its residuals sum to zero over that unit.

A quantile has no design effect, and deff is NA.

Domains

by gives the quantiles of each domain, each from the distribution function of the domain's sampled rows. The variance of F(q) is that of the domain's Hajek mean of y <= q, from the whole sample, as described under "Domains" in ht_total(), and the degrees of freedom are the design's. The result is a drawn_by table with a row for each domain and probability.

Comparison with survey

For the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors, the estimate, the interval and the standard error equal those of survey::svyquantile(ci = TRUE, interval.type = "mean") on its result, whose interval is also centred on F(q) rather than on p. They differ in these places:

  • At the largest sampled value survey gives an interval of no width and a standard error of 0, where ht_quantile() gives none.

  • Where the interval for F(q) passes 0 or 1, survey gives NaN for that end and the standard error, where ht_quantile() gives NA.

  • For a p, or an end of the interval for F(q), below the share of the weight held by the smallest sampled value, survey's rule gives the second smallest value and ht_quantile() the smallest.

  • For a p within 1e-9 above a share of the weight, ht_quantile() gives the value at that share and survey the next one, as "The quantile rule" describes.

  • With by, survey::svyby() with survey::svyquantile() forms each interval on the degrees of freedom of the domain's own units, and ht_quantile() on the design's, as for every domain estimate here. With df = Inf in both, the standard errors agree.

For systematic, spread and systematic PPS samples the variance of F(q) comes from the estimator this package uses for their totals, which survey does not have.

A missing y is refused. survey::svyquantile(na.rm = TRUE) on as_svydesign() estimates the quantiles over the rows that have one.

References

Woodruff, R. S. (1952). Confidence intervals for medians and other position measures. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 47, 635–646.

Särndal, C.-E., Swensson, B. and Wretman, J. (1992). Model Assisted Survey Sampling. Springer.

See also

ht_mean(), ht_total(), as_svydesign()

Examples

set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(
  id = 1:300,
  site = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), each = 100),
  spend = round(stats::rlnorm(300, 4, 0.8))
)
s <- draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 60), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)

# The median, and its Woodruff interval
ht_quantile(s, "spend")
#> Quantile of `spend`  (stratified design, n = 60)
#>   prob     0.5
#>   estimate 55
#>   se       6.741689  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  49 to 76  (Woodruff, t, 57 df)
stats::median(pop$spend)   # the truth
#> [1] 53

# The quartiles of each site, from the whole sample
ht_quantile(s, "spend", probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), by = "site")
#> Quantiles of `spend` by domain  (stratified design, 95% CI, Woodruff, t, 57 df)
#>  site prob  n quantile     se ci_lower ci_upper   method
#>     a 0.25 20       33  9.488       20       58 analytic
#>     a 0.50 20       75 13.733       40       95 analytic
#>     a 0.75 20       95 13.483       86      140 analytic
#>     b 0.25 20       38  5.993       26       50 analytic
#>     b 0.50 20       51  9.239       39       76 analytic
#>     b 0.75 20       76 21.723       53      140 analytic
#>     c 0.25 20       32  8.989       18       54 analytic
#>     c 0.50 20       55 18.977       40      116 analytic
#>     c 0.75 20      116 38.453       62      216 analytic
